name: Kenyan Pilau
description: Pilau depends on real technique across every step: the meat is first boiled separately to build a genuine stock, the onions are deeply browned until dark (this is what naturally colors the whole dish, not a food coloring), and whole spices go in alongside real bay leaves - the rice then cooks directly in that scented broth, absorbing it fully.
steps_detailed: Simmer the beef with the bay leaves, half the ginger, half the garlic, and enough water to cover, 30-35 minutes, until tender. Reserve the broth.
In a separate pot, cook the onion in oil over medium heat, stirring often, 12-15 minutes, until deeply, darkly browned - this real browning is what colors the entire dish.
Add the remaining ginger and garlic, and the cumin, cinnamon, and cardamom, and cook 1-2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the rice and the reserved broth (adding water if needed to reach 1.25 cups total liquid), along with the cooked beef.
Cover and simmer on low 18-20 minutes without lifting the lid, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.

steps_detailed: Whisk the cornmeal into 1.25 cups boiling water.

name: Kenyan Sukuma Wiki
description: Sukuma wiki, collard greens or kale simmered with onion and tomato, is one of Kenya's most essential everyday side dishes - its name means 'to stretch the week', reflecting its role as an affordable, real everyday staple, not an afterthought.
steps_detailed: Cook the onion 4-5 minutes, then add the tomatoes and simmer 3-4 minutes.
Add the kale and simmer 10-12 minutes until tender.

name: Kenyan Nyama Choma
description: Nyama choma, meaning 'grilled meat', is central to Kenyan social eating, traditionally cooked slowly over charcoal and served simply, letting the real char and smoke carry the flavor rather than a heavy marinade.
steps_detailed: Rub the beef with the garlic and lemon juice.
Grill over medium-high heat, turning, 12-15 minutes, until well charred and cooked through.

name: Kenyan Chapati
description: Chapati, a soft, layered flatbread, reflects genuine Indian culinary influence along the Kenyan coast and beyond - real technique coiling the rolled dough before flattening again is what builds true flaky layers.
steps_detailed: Work the flour with warm water and half the oil into a soft dough. Rest 20 minutes.
Roll thin, brush with the remaining oil, and coil before flattening again to build real layers.
Cook in a hot, dry pan, 2-3 minutes per side, until golden.

Fry, turning, 3-4 minutes per batch, until deeply golden.
